content_metadata.description: An educational video providing a detailed examination of blood cells using microscopic footage. The video covers the characteristics, morphology, and functions of different blood cell types.

qAndA.answer: Erythrocytes are flexible and biconcave discs.
qAndA.question: What is the shape of an erythrocyte?

qAndA.answer: Monocytes are the largest type of leukocyte.
qAndA.question: Which leukocyte is the largest in size?

qAndA.answer: Granulocytes are classified into three types based on the staining characteristics of their granules: neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.
qAndA.question: How are granulocytes classified?

qAndA.answer: The biconcave shape of the erythrocyte causes a thinner central area, allowing more light to pass through, creating a lighter halo.
qAndA.question: Why is the central area of an erythrocyte lighter in color when viewed under a microscope?

qAndA.answer: Platelets are actively involved in blood clotting.
qAndA.question: What is the main function of platelets?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: In the differential staining, we can distinguish cellular structures according to the affinity
for basic dyes, assets or a mixture of both.
When placing the smear under the microscope, it is convenient to initially determine
which area of the smear we are observing, head, body or tail.
As we scan the sample, we are able to see the appearance of the cells.
In the head of the sample, the area in which the drop was placed, a greater cellularity
is observed.
The uthrocytes will be very close, forming aggravates and the coloration becomes grayish.
This zone should be avoided in order to be able to distinguish the different cell types present.
As we scan the sample in the direction of the extension, the concentration of cells
will decrease.
The optimum area will be the center or body of the smear.
The cells are more separated and the actual coloration acquired by the blood of the smear
can be seen with the gym's staining.
Blood blood cells appear pink, leuker cells show the nuclei staining purple and their
cytoplasm impale pink.
As you will expect, the most abundant cell type is the uthrocyte.
It represents 99% of the blood cells.
They are flexible and via concave discs.
They lack a cell nucleus.
The shape is the one that causes a clear halo or descentral of the cell when the light
of the microscope closes it.
This morphology provides essential properties for physiological cell function such as deformability
and stability when traveling the circular toll system, and specifically the capillary network.
In addition, it maximizes the surface for cellular gas exchange.
As you can see in the right image, the uthrocyte of other spaces may have different characteristics.
In this case, an ellipse of dye and nucleated uthrocyte extension is shown very different
from the human ones.
At a higher magnification, the uthrocyte morphology is clearly seen.
White blood cells, also called leuker cells, are shown.
They are the cells of the immune system that are involved in protecting the body against
both infection disease and foreign invaders.
Monocytes are the largest type of leukocyte.
They contain kidney-shaped lurved nuclei, and these cells are able to migrate to tissues
where they will differentiate into tissue macrophages when needed.
We continue scanning the preparation and looking at the cells' types present.
The lymphocyte is the smallest of the leuker cells.
All the different types of lymphocytes exist such as B cells, T cells, and natural killers.
Immunihistochemical techniques are required to differentiate them.
Vinyl sites, also called polymol for nuclear leukocytes, are characterized by the presence
of granules in their cytoplasm.
They are divided into three types according to the staining characteristics of their granules.
Neutrophils, ears and filth, and basophils.
The most abundant in human blood are neutrophils.
These granules are not observed with this type of staining.
Eosinfilth and basophils are less frequent.
Playlets can also be found which are cytoplasmic fragments of the precursor cell, the mega-carosit.
They are actively involved in clotting and may be found isolated or cloted.
They are infrequent in these samples because this mirror was click-knit on right after

Here, a polymol for nuclear cells can be seen characterized by having abundant granules
that do not allow us to see the polymorphic nucleus.

youtube_description:
Autor: Serna García, Eva; Megías Vericat, Javier; San Miguel Diez, Teresa
Serie: Recursos didácticos y complementarios para estudiantes de Biología
Data: 2017
Resum: This project is for the students of the Biology Unit (Department of Pathology) from the degrees of Health Sciences. One of the objectives is to provide complementary multimedia material to prepare and better understand the laboratory practices and, on the other hand, to consolidate the knowledge that will be developed throughout it. To this end, this video describes in virtual way the visualization of different cellular types of samples obtained in a human blood smear.
